newsitem.title: GREECE: Greenpeace activists charged over refinery protest.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace activists charged over refinery protest.

text.p: A Greek prosecutor charged 17 Greenpeace activists on Wednesday over their 24-hour blockade of Motor Oil, Greece's biggest oil refinery.
It is the first time Greece has brought criminal charges against the international environmental group, which blockaded the refinery's port to demand stricter laws against oil pollution.

Corinth head prosecutor Nikolaos Pandelis told reporters he had charged the activists with trespassing and hindering a public service company, and scheduled their trial for February 6. They were all set free.
If convicted they face up to five years in jail.
"It was the first time in my career that the defendants asked to spend the night in jail and be tried immediately. I saw no reason to agree and set a later date," he said.
The activists, who include people from Britain, Austria and Germany, had asked for summary legal procedures because they would be on other Greenpeace missions during the winter.
"I'll be in Antarctica for a climate campaign," said Simon Ayloff from England.
Scores of residents of the city southwest of Athens applauded and cheered as the activists left the prosecutors' office, shouting slogans such as "Hands off Greenpeace".
Earlier in the day coast guard commandos removed the demonstrators from the port near the Corinth canal after cutting through chains pinning them to mooring buoys and loading cranes.
Motor Oil, which employs about 1,300 people and had a 1994 turnover of about $750 million, had demanded they be removed.
"They are risking the safety of this refinery, which has not been designed to deal with lunatics," Motor Oil representative Constantine Vassilakis said.
Greenpeace began its protest early on Tuesday, accusing Motor Oil of being lax on environmental safety by allowing loading at night and during bad weather.
It says a major oil spill at the refinery in August was the latest in a long series of mishaps and wants the government to lay down stricter laws on oil pollution.

The refinery denies responsibility for the accident, blaming sudden bad weather and the docked ship, which was also owned by Motor Oil. It says it usually takes measures stricter than those required by Greek law.
Greek opposition parties condemned the raid on the Greenpeace activists, saying the government used a military-type operation to protect Motor Oil instead of pushing for better safety laws.

"We asked the government, instead of arrests and violence against environmental groups, to explain its refusal to push tough safety rules and adopt Greenpeace's proposals on oil pollution," the Left Coalition party said in a statement.
The party said it would bring the matter before the Greek parliament.
The blockade had frozen operations for 24 hours at the refinery, which is jointly owned by Saudi Aramco and the Vardiniyannis group and can handle about five million tonnes of fuel annually.

Aramco bought a 50 percent stake in the Vardinoyannis family's Motor Oil Corinth Refineries SA and the accompanying Avinoil Industries distribution network in Greece for $379 million earlier this year.
The Greenpeace ship Arctic Sunrise, which had helped block access to the refinery, was moved away and its captain David Enever was among those arrested.
Enever was also arrested by French authorities as captain of the Rainbow Warrior during an anti-nuclear protest at Mururoa Atoll in the South Pacific in July 1995, Greenpeace said.
